The most recent polls, all taken within the final week or so before the November 3 election, show a close race with a slight Talarico edge in most of them.

- **NYT/Siena (Oct. 27 to Nov. 1):** Talarico led Paxton 50% to 43%, a 7-point gap that is well outside the error margin for this poll.
- **Quantus Insights (reported Oct. 30):** This was the outlier. The Quantus poll found that 48.7% of respondents backed Paxton, while 47.6% backed Talarico.
- **ActiVote (Oct. 22 to 28, published Oct. 29):** Talarico led 52.1% to 47.9%, a 4.2-point gap. Compared with our October 21 poll, Talarico's lead widened from 2.0% to 4.2%.
- **Marist (Oct. 8 to 11):** Talarico led 47% to 45% among likely voters, down from a 6-point lead the prior month.
- **Hobby School, University of Houston (reported Oct. 18):** Talarico led 48% to 46%, with 3% for Libertarian Ted Brown.

Taken together, the polls point to a narrow Talarico lead, with one late poll showing Paxton slightly ahead. Individual poll margins of error are around 4 to 5 points, so the race looks close to a toss-up. These are pre-election polls, so the result itself is not yet known from these sources.

Early voting in Texas's November 3, 2026 general election has ended, and the total is about 7.7 million voters, a record for a midterm. Sources differ slightly on the exact count and cutoff date.

- **Texas Tribune:** More than 7.7 million Texans voted early in the 2026 midterm election, according to preliminary data from the secretary of state's office as of Sunday morning. That puts turnout at 40.5%, surpassing the modern-day high-water mark for a midterm election set in 2018.
- **Secretary of State data via TexPolls:** Through October 30, 2026 (day 12 of 12), the Texas Secretary of State reports 7,711,768 Texans have voted early, 40.5% of 19,041,684 registered voters.
- **theoelections.com:** reports 7,744,549 Texans have voted as of Oct 30, 2026: 7,463,553 early in person and 280,996 by mail.
- **TransparencyUSA:** shows 7,710,526 votes cast and 40.1% turnout, using a registration base of 19,228,703 (this page may have been captured at a different time).

The differences come from the registration denominator and the date each tracker was pulled. Early voting totals will not include Election Day ballots, so the final turnout will be higher. One analyst quoted by the Tribune said, "How many votes are actually still out there?"

Recent October 2026 polls show Abbott ahead of Hinojosa, but by a shrinking margin in most of them.

- **Texas Public Opinion Research (released Oct. 23):** Abbott led 51% to 48%, with his lead down from 7 points in August and 4 in September. Libertarian Pat Dixon receiving 1% of the vote.
- **University of Houston Hobby School (Oct. 10–14, 2,000 likely voters):** Abbott had 49% and Hinojosa 46%, with a margin of error of ±2.19 points. Undecided: 3%
- **ActiVote (released Oct. 29):** Abbott led 52.1% to 47.9%, with his lead narrowing from 5.0 points on Oct. 21. Compared with our October 21 poll, Abbott's lead narrowed from 5.0% to 4.2%.
- **Texas Southern University (released Oct. 29):** Hinojosa had 47% of respondents, and Abbott's favorability was 48% to her 45%. Independents broke for Hinojosa by 11 points.
- **GBAO (Hinojosa-aligned, Oct. 13):** This poll had Hinojosa ahead 47% to 45%. Its findings were released by the Hinojosa campaign, so treat it with caution.

The Texas Public Opinion Research and ActiVote polls are the most recent. The Hobby School poll is from mid-October, and the Texas Southern and GBAO polls are the most partisan or least recent. Pollsters differ on the size of Abbott's lead, but most show him ahead by low single digits. The election is on November 3, 2026.

Census data put August 2026 private data center construction at about $85 billion at a seasonally adjusted annual rate, up roughly 73% from a year earlier.

- **August figure:** The Census release from October 1, 2026 put the rate at $84.95 billion, with July revised to $79 billion. The 7.5 percent monthly gain was measured against July, and the rate was 73.2 percent above August 2025. Private data center spending rose from $49.05 billion to $84.95 billion year over year.
- **Scope:** The Census definitions leave out the value of racks or servers, so the figure covers buildings and related work. Power plants and transmission lines for data center demand are counted in a separate power category.
- **Total construction:** Total construction spending was $2,203.1 billion at an annual rate, up 0.9 percent on the month and down 1.7 percent from a year earlier.
- **Newer release:** A later Census report, published November 2, 2026, puts September at a record $96.5 billion annual rate. That is preliminary, and the August figure has since been revised. The same release shows the September rate was up 90.3% from a year earlier, while total construction spending fell 1.9%.
- **Caveat:** One Census-based article says a $28.5 billion figure that circulated earlier does not match the Census data, so that number should be ignored.

I couldn't find an October 2026 approved-to-energize figure in these results. The most recent data points are from May and September 2026, and they point to a pause on energization.

- **Energization pause (most recent):** ERCOT's September 2026 Batch Zero update says the grid operator has paused approvals to energize data centers and crypto mining facilities of 75 MW or more (index 2-6). A separate gr1d page, updated about a week ago, lists Oct. 19–20, 2026 TCEQ actions and a Nov. 1 quarterly stability screen covering 17 loads, about 6,874 MW. It describes that screen as a requirement, not an energization approval (index 8-3).
- **Approved to energize (May 2026):** A ERCOT LLWG meeting summary from May 21 reports roughly 9,062 MW approved to energize over the prior 12 months (index 5-6). The same summary puts non-simultaneous peak consumption near 3,900 MW in May 2026, and simultaneous peak near 3,701 MW (indices 5-7, 5-8).
- **Earlier baseline (March 2026):** A ERCOT March 2026 status report lists 9,042 MW approved to energize, with about 3,883 MW non-simultaneous peak observed (index 1-6). Another analysis from March 2026 puts approved-to-energize but not operational at 3,241 MW, and observed energized load at 5,778 MW (index 9-5).
- **Queue size:** ERCOT's June 2026 update says it is tracking about 438 GW of large-load requests under the older process, which ends July 10, 2026, when batch-based processing starts (index 4-6, 4-11). A June tracker lists the queue at 238.6 GW as of March 2026 (index 7-1).

Caveat: the gr1d and interconnectionqueue.org sources are third-party trackers, so the official ERCOT documents are the better reference for specific figures. The ERCOT pages I found are dated March, May, and September 2026, not October.

The main result is New York. Its legislature passed a statewide data center moratorium bill, but the governor's response took a different form.

- **The bill:** The New York legislature passed the Responsible Data Center Development Act on June 4, 2026, with the Senate voting 44–16 and the Assembly 102–39. It would impose a one-year pause on state permits for large facilities drawing 20 megawatts or more (new large data centers with peak demand of 20 megawatts or more). It also covers hyperscale facilities.
- **Governor's action:** Per one law firm's account, Governor Kathy Hochul did not sign the bill. Instead, on July 14, 2026, she signed the narrower Executive Order No. 62. That order imposes a one-year moratorium on discretionary environmental permitting for data centers expected to draw more than 50 megawatts of power, a higher threshold than the legislature's 20 MW.
- **Source conflict:** Some sources are older and still describe the bill as awaiting her decision. For example, one tracker lists it as awaiting a response from Governor Kathy Hochul. The WilmerHale account is more recent, so I'd treat the executive order as the current status, but I couldn't confirm it against a primary government source in this search.
- **Other states:** Maine is not a counterexample to the "first" claim. Its moratorium bill, LD 307, was vetoed by the governor of Maine, Janet Mills, after it passed both legislative houses on April 14.

Links: [{"title":"Texas lawmakers consider ending billion-dollar data center tax break","url":"https://communityimpact.com/central-austin/texas-legislature/texas-spends-billions-on-tax-breaks-for-data-centers-theres-a-bipartisan-legislative-push-to-repeal-them/"},{"title":"Texas Will Change the Data Center Sales Tax Exemption in 2027 Based on Numbers Drafted in August","url":"https://x.com/jamesdickey/article/2082152492389876070"},{"title":"Texas losing a billion dollars a year on data center tax break","url":"https://www.texastribune.org/2026/04/08/texas-data-centers-sales-tax-break-billion-dollars/"},{"title":"Texas lawmakers scrutinize $3.3 billion cost of data center tax incentives","url":"https://www.krqe.com/news/national/texas-lawmakers-scrutinize-3-3-billion-cost-of-data-center-tax-incentives/"},{"title":"Texas Data Center Tax Breaks Top $1 Billion a Year","url":"https://www.governing.com/finance/texas-data-center-tax-breaks-top-1-billion-a-year"},{"title":"State Data Center Policy: Governors Restrict Tax Exemptions","url":"https://www.multistate.us/insider/2026/6/22/state-data-center-policy-shifts-as-governors-impose-new-restrictions"},{"title":"Texas sales tax exemption for AI data centers · Compute Law Blog","url":"https://computelaw.blog/tax/texas-sales-tax-exemption-ai-data-centers/"},{"title":"Texas is giving data centers more than $1 billion in tax breaks each year","url":"https://www.ketk.com/news/texas/texas-is-giving-data-centers-more-than-1-billion-in-tax-breaks-each-year/"},{"title":"www.texastribune.org","url":"https://www.texastribune.org/?p=226019"},{"title":"Texas is giving data centers more than $1 billion in tax breaks each year","url":"https://www.aol.com/news/texas-giving-data-centers-more-173020114.html"}]

Here's what the search turned up. The main point is that repeal is now a serious 2027 proposal, but no bill has been filed yet.

- **Cost:** The comptroller's office estimates the exemption will cost Texas $3.2 billion in sales tax revenue over the next two years. A later figure from a Senate Finance hearing put the cost at $3.3 billion in forgone taxes by the 2028-29 budget cycle. Projections keep rising: an annual cost approaching $1.8 billion by fiscal year 2030. The original estimate was much lower, since the comptroller had projected the tax break would be valued at about $180 million in the 2027-2028 biennial budget.
- **Repeal push:** Senate Finance Chair Joan Huffman has said she plans to look at filing legislation to either repeal the exemption or take a very close look at it. Governor Abbott has also listed repeal among his 2027 legislative priorities. Lawmakers could also reduce it, further limit the number of years it remains in effect, or tie the tax break to stronger economic development requirements.
- **Hearing status:** The July Senate Finance interim hearing produced no legislation. Lawmakers indicated the future of Texas' data center tax incentives will likely be a topic of debate when lawmakers return to Austin in 2027.
- **Scope:** The exemption covers the state's sales tax on qualifying purchases and also exempts data centers from paying state sales taxes on the cost of electricity. A narrower option that has been discussed is excluding electricity, since twenty-two of the 36 peer sales tax states already exclude electricity.
- **Timing and uncertainty:** The Legislature doesn't convene until January 2027. Also, it remains uncertain whether the legislature would apply a repeal to already certified facilities.

Caveats: The Texas Tribune and Communities Impact pieces are the most reliable here. The James Dickey item is an x.com post, so treat its details as unverified. The search didn't surface a final comptroller estimate for a repeal scenario.

Here's what the results show about the Abbott pause, the audit, and the Hinojosa campaign.

- **Scope of the pause:** Abbott ordered regulators to stop approving new data center grid connections in August, and later ordered the state environmental agency to halt data center-related permits until ERCOT finishes its waitlist audit. The pause reaches about 300 large projects but not medium-sized or smaller ones, or parts of the state off the ERCOT grid, and the audit it hangs on isn't expected to wrap until mid-December.
- **Tax incentives:** The audit covers state and local tax incentives, grants, and abatements that data centers receive or expect to receive. Abbott's press release said that next session he will work with the Legislature to eliminate any financial incentives for data centers.
- **Abbott's position:** He says the pause since he put it in place has worked.
- **Hinojosa's position:** She has said that he can change his mind November 4th, and she called the pause "an election year stunt." She wants to end sales tax exemptions for large data centers. Her campaign also wants the pause extended, not canceled. She has said "We are not asking the Governor to cancel the audit." Pause all of it, publish what you find, and tell us when the pause ends.
- **Donations:** A Texas Tribune analysis found Abbott received about $9 million from data center-related donors since July 2025, including $2.8 million after announcing the pause.
- **Race status:** Polls show the race neck-and-neck, and Abbott's campaign has poured $117 million into ads — more than four times as much as Hinojosa.

The sources conflict on timing. ERCOT indicated its audits would take until at least December, and Hinojosa has questioned the timing of the review.

**Statewide data center moratoria (14 states, status as of June 8, 2026)**

| State (Bill) | Scope and Duration | Size Threshold | Status and Date |
|---|---|---|---|
| Georgia (HB 1059) | Bars local governments from permitting data centers until December 2028 | None specified | Introduced |
| Maine (LD 307) | Moratorium until November 2027 | 20 MW | Vetoed by Gov. Mills, April 24, 2026 |
| Maryland (HB 120) | Prohibits construction and permitting | None specified | Introduced |
| Michigan (HB 5594/5595) | Bars local governments and the Public Service Commission from permitting or approving until April 2027 | None specified | Introduced |
| Minnesota (HB 4888/SB 4298) | Blocks new permits until the Public Utility Commission submits a report, at least until July 2027 | 100 MW | Introduced |
| New Hampshire (HB 1265) | One-year pause on construction | None specified | Introduced |
| New York (AB 10141/SB 9144) | One-year pause on siting, construction, or operation of new data centers | 20 MW | Passed the Legislature June 4, 2026; awaiting Gov. Hochul |
| Oklahoma (SB 1488) | Prohibits construction until November 2029 | 100 MW | Introduced |
| Virginia (HB 1515) | Pauses new data centers until interconnection requests are fulfilled or July 2028 | 1 MW | Introduced |
| Pennsylvania (HB 2533) | Three-year moratorium on new "high impact" data centers | 25 MW | Introduced |
| South Carolina (H 5526) | Bars local approval until the Legislature adopts an oversight framework | 5 MW | Introduced |
| South Dakota (SB 232) | Pauses new construction or expansion of hyperscale data centers until June 30, 2027 | 50 MW | Introduced |
| Vermont (S 205) | Impact study and moratorium on siting and construction of AI data centers until 2030 | 100 MW | Introduced |
| Wisconsin (SB 1061/AB 1099) | Bars operation of data centers until certain conditions are met | 100 MW | Introduced |

**Pending in 2027 sessions:** The article does not say which bills will carry over into 2027 or which legislatures will take them up. Several moratoria would run into 2027 (Michigan, Minnesota, South Dakota, and Maine's vetoed bill), but those are end dates for the pauses, not session timing. The New York bill is the only one with a clear next step: the governor's response.

**Notes:**
- The article's table has some incorrect links. For example, the Maryland HB 120 link points to Maine's LD 307.
- Local moratoria, such as those in Lysander and Perth, are excluded because they are not statewide.

I ran one search and did not find any August, September, or October 2026 figures. The latest material is from around June 2026, so the approved-to-energize numbers below are dated.

The January 2026 ERCOT TAC meeting highlighted three structural shifts in the ERCOT market: Large Load Interconnection Status: Large load queue declined slightly due to project cancellations. • Approval to Energize: 8,786 MW.
- **March 2026:** A tracker site citing the March 2026 TAC report gives 9,042 MW approved to energize and 3,883 MW observed operating. It also notes that ERCOT's tracked large-load queue has grown roughly 11.5× since 2022 — to about 439 GW, around 87% data centers.
- **April 2026 ERCOT Monthly:** ERCOT reported 5.9 GW of Observed Energized Large Loads, with another 3.2 GW of loads that have Approval to Energize but are not Operational. This split differs from the tracker's framing, so the two sources should not be combined.
- **Batch Zero:** On June 18, 2026, the Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT) approved two Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) protocol revisions that establish a new "batch" study interconnection framework for large electricity loads of 75 MW or larger.
